findings.title: Device is cached before the limit check, so the limit is bypassed after the first request
findings.body: `tagDeviceUI` calls `a.localCache.SetDefault(key, ...)` before `CreateOrUpdateDevice`, and keeps the entry when that call returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. Only the first request from a new device over the limit is rejected. For the next ~29 minutes (cache TTL), `localCache.Get(key)` hits, `tagDeviceUI` returns nil, and `Anonymous.Authenticate` lets the device in. The device is never stored or counted, so a user who just reloads the page is admitted. The cache entry should only be set after a successful create/update, or removed on `ErrDeviceLimitReached`.

findings.title: Check-then-insert race lets the device count exceed the limit
findings.body: `CreateOrUpdateDevice` runs `CountDevices` in one session and the INSERT/upsert in a separate session, with no transaction or locking. When the count is just under the limit, several concurrent requests from new devices (on one instance or across HA instances) can all see `count < deviceLimit` and all insert. The limit can therefore be exceeded by the level of concurrency. If it is meant as a hard cap, the check and insert need to be atomic, e.g. a conditional INSERT ... SELECT with the count in the WHERE clause, or a transaction with appropriate locking.

findings.title: Device limit is trivially bypassed by omitting the device ID header
findings.body: Enforcement depends on `TagDevice` returning `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. `TagDevice` returns nil early when the client-controlled `X-Grafana-Device-Id` header is missing (and also when the remote address can't be parsed). In both cases `Anonymous.Authenticate` succeeds. Any client that does not send the header (curl, scripts, a modified frontend) gets anonymous access regardless of the configured limit, and is never counted. If the limit is meant to be enforced, requests without a device ID should be handled explicitly once the limit is reached.

findings.title: Device tagging moved into the request path unconditionally, even when no limit is set
findings.body: The goroutine with its own timeout and panic recovery was replaced by a synchronous `TagDevice(ctx, ...)` call for every deployment, including the default `device_limit = 0`. Every anonymous request that misses the local cache now waits for a DB upsert before authentication completes. With a limit set, it also waits for an extra `COUNT(*)` over `anon_device`. The panic recovery was also dropped. Consider keeping the asynchronous path when `AnonymousDeviceLimit == 0` and only blocking when enforcement is needed.

findings.title: DI wiring for AnonStore likely broken by the ProvideAnonDBStore signature change
findings.body: `ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` used to receive `anonstore.AnonStore` via dependency injection, so a provider for it (`anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` plus a bind) was registered in the wire set. `ProvideAnonDBStore` now requires an `int64`, which wire cannot supply, and the service no longer consumes `AnonStore`. `pkg/server/wire.go` is not updated in this PR. Wire generation will fail either on the unsatisfiable `int64` or on an unused provider, unless that registration is removed. Any other single-argument callers of `ProvideAnonDBStore` will also fail to compile.

findings.title: New `device_limit` setting is undocumented and missing from the default/sample config
findings.body: `[auth.anonymous] device_limit` is read here, but the PR adds no entry to `conf/defaults.ini` / `conf/sample.ini` and no documentation. Operators have no way to discover the option. Nothing tells them that 0 means unlimited, that devices are counted over a 30-day window, or that anonymous users over the limit are rejected at authentication.

findings.title: anonymousDeviceLimit is inferred as type `undefined` on GrafanaBootConfig
findings.body: `anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined;` has no type annotation, so with strictNullChecks TypeScript infers the property type as `undefined` rather than `number | undefined`. It still satisfies `implements GrafanaConfig`, but consumers of `config.anonymousDeviceLimit` see a type that can never hold a number. The backend always sends an int64 (0 when unset), so the value is never actually undefined. Annotate it, e.g. `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined = undefined;`.

findings.title: Limit tests don't cover updating existing devices at the limit or the service/cache path
findings.body: `TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only checks that a second, new device is rejected. It does not check that an already-registered device can still be updated (the `updateDevice` happy path) once the limit is reached. No test exercises the limit through `AnonDeviceService.TagDevice` / `Anonymous.Authenticate`. Such a test would have caught that the local cache lets a rejected device through on its next request.
